### BoK Gate check (v3 — MCORCH Master Execution Protocol)

For each BoK suite in `docs/bok/<slug>/`, verify completeness:
```bash
for slug in $(ls docs/bok/ 2>/dev/null); do
  if [ "$slug" = "security" ]; then
    required_sec=(00-deepsearch-blueprint 01-brd-security 02-srs-secure-spec 03-sdd-hardening-architecture 04-fmea-security)
    missing=()
    for doc in "${required_sec[@]}"; do
      [ -f "docs/bok/security/$doc.md" ] || missing+=("$doc")
    done
    [ ${#missing[@]} -eq 0 ] && echo "✅ security — BoK complete (ciso-4-artifact)" || echo "⚠️ security — missing: ${missing[*]}"
    continue
  fi
  required=(00-index 01-mrd 02-brd 03-prd 04-frd 05-sdd 06-data-model 07-process-flow 08-quality-metrics)
  missing=()
  for doc in "${required[@]}"; do
    [ -f "docs/bok/$slug/$doc.md" ] || missing+=("$doc")
  done
  [ ${#missing[@]} -eq 0 ] && echo "✅ $slug — BoK complete" || echo "⚠️ $slug — missing: ${missing[*]}"
done
```

If the user mentions working on a **new module / complex feature / integration / architectural change**:

## Rules

- **TypeScript errors → report immediately.** If there are TS errors, list them under ALERTAS. Do not start implementing new features until errors are resolved (unless the user explicitly asks to proceed despite errors).
- **Unhealthy containers → report with triage.** Suggest the fix command if known (e.g., `docker compose restart mcorch-vector-engine` for chroma).
- **Uncommitted changes → describe, do not commit.** Only describe what exists in the working tree; committing is the user's call.
- **Keep the brief tight.** No padding. No repetition of CLAUDE.md architecture. The user already knows the architecture — they need the delta: what changed, what's broken, what's next.
- **Pending Actions priority order:** CRITICAL (before first client) > NON-CRITICAL > Phase Zeta > Core v3 > Epsilon v9.
- **Knowledge Mesh numbers:** use `GraphRAG State` section from HANDOFF.md as the source. Do not invent counts.

  "old_string": "import { MessageRow } from \"@/hooks/useConversations\";\nimport { useSignedMediaUrl } from \"@/lib/asset-url\";\nimport {\n  FileText, Image, Mic, File, Tag, Video, Smile, MapPin, User, Download,\n  Loader2, AlertTriangle, Check, CheckCheck,\n} from \"lucide-react\";",
  "new_string": "import { MessageRow } from \"@/hooks/useConversations\";\nimport { useSignedMediaUrl } from \"@/lib/asset-url\";\nimport { toast } from \"sonner\";\nimport {\n  FileText, Image, Mic, File, Tag, Video, Smile, MapPin, User, Download,\n  Loader2, AlertTriangle, Check, CheckCheck, Copy, MessageCircle, Phone,\n} from \"lucide-react\";\n\n/**\n * Parse a WhatsApp-shared contact vCard (base64, VERSION:3.0) best-effort. The webhook stores the raw\n * `contacts[]` payload; the structured `name`/`phones` fields cover name + number, but the business\n * description (X-WA-BIZ-DESCRIPTION, e.g. \"UX/UI/AI Designer\") lives ONLY inside the vCard blob. Never\n * throws \u2014 a malformed/undecodable card just yields an empty object.\n */\nfunction parseVCard(b64?: unknown): { name?: string; phone?: string; waid?: string; description?: string } {\n  if (typeof b64 !== \"string\" || !b64) return {};\n  let text: string;\n  try {\n    const bin = atob(b64);\n    text = new TextDecoder(\"utf-8\").decode(Uint8Array.from(bin, (ch) => ch.charCodeAt(0)));\n  } catch {\n    return {};\n  }\n  const out: { name?: string; phone?: string; waid?: string; description?: string } = {};\n  for (const line of text.split(/\\r?\\n/)) {\n    if (line.startsWith(\"FN:\")) out.name = line.slice(3).trim();\n    else if (line.startsWith(\"X-WA-BIZ-DESCRIPTION:\")) out.description = line.slice(21).trim();\n    else if (line.startsWith(\"TEL\")) {\n      const idx = line.lastIndexOf(\":\");\n      if (idx >= 0 && !out.phone) out.phone = line.slice(idx + 1).trim();\n      const waid = line.match(/waid=(\\d+)/);\n      if (waid && !out.waid) out.waid = waid[1];\n    }\n  }\n  return out;\n}"
}

<EyeOff className=\"h-3.5 w-3.5\" /> : <Eye className=\"h-3.5 w-3.5\" />}\n          </button>\n        </div>\n        {testable && <Button\n          type=\"button\"\n          variant=\"outline\"\n          size=\"sm\"\n          onClick={handleTest}\n          disabled={status === \"testing\" || !value.trim()}\n          className=\"shrink-0 gap-1.5 text-xs\"\n        >\n          {status === \"testing\" ? ## 🤖 Claude *(03:47:19)*

<details>
<summary>💭 Thinking Process</summary>

Exit code 144 is 128 plus 16, which corresponds to SIGTERM. The `pkill -f "vite preview"` command might have terminated the bash process itself since it matches against the full command line, though pkill typically excludes its own process from matches—but it's possible it caught the parent shell or interrupted the command chain before completion.

I should try a different approach: instead of using pkill with a pattern that could self-match, I'll kill the preview process by targeting the specific port it's running on, and check git status separately to avoid any process interruption.

</details>

<details>
<summary>💭 Thinking Process</summary>

Moving on to FR-CRM-028, which adds emoji reactions to WhatsApp balloons. I need to implement two parts: a server-side action in the templates that posts to Meta's API with the message ID and emoji, plus UI hover interactions on inbound messages since reactions already render on the client.

For the backend, I'm creating the reaction action that sends to Meta's messaging endpoint with the reaction type and target message details, then persisting an outbound message record with the reaction metadata. There's some nuance around whether reactions respect the 24-hour customer service window — Meta's docs suggest they do since reactions are technically messages, but the requirements specify window-agnostic behavior, so I'll implement it permissively and allow reactions on active conversations.

Now I need to examine the existing `send` and `mark_read` actions to match their patterns for auth, meta_config resolution, the POST request shape, and message persistence. On the client side, I'm building a hook like `useSendReaction` that takes the conversation, target message ID, and emoji, then calls the backend action.

For the UI, when hovering over an inbound message balloon, I'll show a reaction picker with a few quick emoji options (👍❤️😂😮😢🙏). To keep things consistent with how inbound reactions already render as separate "Reagiu com X" bubbles, I'll insert outbound reactions the same way—as a message row with `content_type=reaction` and `direction=outbound`—rather than trying to overlay badges like WhatsApp's native UI does. action persists as an outbound reaction message. This keeps the scope minimal and aligned with what's already working for inbound reactions, avoiding a larger refactor of the badge-overlay system. I'm realizing that WhatsApp reactions have a quirk—sending an empty emoji actually removes a reaction, and only one reaction per message is allowed at a time. For the MVP, I'll keep it straightforward: support sending a reaction with an emoji, and maybe add a toggle to remove it if the operator already reacted. Keeping the scope tight for now.

Reactions are free (0 mco), and Meta doesn't charge for them within an open conversation. Now I need to look at the existing `send` and `mark_read` server actions to understand the pattern—how they resolve meta_config, handle phone_id and token, make the POST request, and insert the message with tenant scoping. Let me examine the whatsapp-templates file to see how those are structured.

</details>

Free + window-agnostic; the edge fn binds the\n * target wamid to the owned thread and records the outbound reaction (renders as \"Reagiu com X\").\n */\nexport function useSendReaction() {\n  const queryClient = useQueryClient();\n\n  return useMutation<{ ok: true; removed: boolean }, Error, SendReactionRequest>({\n    mutationFn: async (req) => {\n      const { data: { session } } = await supabase.auth.getSession();\n      if (!session?.access_token) throw new Error(\"N\u00e3o autenticado\");\n\n      const res = await fetch(`${import.meta.env.VITE_SUPABASE_URL}/functions/v1/whatsapp-templates`, {\n        method: \"POST\",\n        headers: {\n          \"Content-Type\": \"application/json\",\n          Authorization: `Bearer ${session.access_token}`,\n        },\n        body: JSON.stringify({\n          action: \"reaction\",\n          conversation_id: req.conversationId,\n          message_id: req.messageId,\n          emoji: req.emoji,\n        }),\n      });\n\n      const json = await res.json();\n      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(edgeErrorMessage(json) || json.error || \"Falha ao reagir\");\n      return json as { ok: true; removed: boolean };\n    },\n    onSuccess: (_data, variables) => {\n      queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: [\"messages\", variables.conversationId] });\n    },\n  });\n}\n\n/** Template cost class helper for UI */"

+/**
+ * Parse a WhatsApp-shared contact vCard (base64, VERSION:3.0) best-effort. The webhook stores the raw
+ * `contacts[]` payload; the structured `name`/`phones` fields cover name + number, but the business
+ * description (X-WA-BIZ-DESCRIPTION, e.g. "UX/UI/AI Designer") lives ONLY inside the vCard blob. Never
+ * throws — a malformed/undecodable card just yields an empty object.
+ */
+function parseVCard(b64?: unknown): { name?: string; phone?: string; waid?: string; description?: string } {
+  if (typeof b64 !== "string" || !b64) return {};
+  let text: string;
+  try {
+    const bin = atob(b64);
+    text = new TextDecoder("utf-8").decode(Uint8Array.from(bin, (ch) => ch.charCodeAt(0)));
+  } catch {
+    return {};
+  }
+  const out: { name?: string; phone?: string; waid?: string; description?: string } = {};
+  for (const line of text.split(/\r?\n/)) {
+    if (line.startsWith("FN:")) out.name = line.slice(3).trim();
+    else if (line.startsWith("X-WA-BIZ-DESCRIPTION:")) out.description = line.slice(21).trim();
+    else if (line.startsWith("TEL")) {
+      const idx = line.lastIndexOf(":");
+      if (idx >= 0 && !out.phone) out.phone = line.slice(idx + 1).trim();
+      const waid = line.match(/waid=(\d+)/);
+      if (waid && !out.waid) out.waid = waid[1];
+    }
+  }
+  return out;
+}

Review the complete diff above. This contains all code changes in the PR.


OBJECTIVE:
Perform a security-focused code review to identify HIGH-CONFIDENCE security vulnerabilities that could have real exploitation potential. This is not a general code review - focus ONLY on security implications newly added by this PR. Do not comment on existing security concerns.

CRITICAL INSTRUCTIONS:
1. MINIMIZE FALSE POSITIVES: Only flag issues where you're >80% confident of actual exploitability
2. AVOID NOISE: Skip theoretical issues, style concerns, or low-impact findings
3. FOCUS ON IMPACT: Prioritize vulnerabilities that could lead to unauthorized access, data breaches, or system compromise
4. EXCLUSIONS: Do NOT report the following issue types:
   - Denial of Service (DOS) vulnerabilities, even if they allow service disruption
   - Secrets or sensitive data stored on disk (these are handled by other processes)
   - Rate limiting or resource exhaustion issues

SECURITY CATEGORIES TO EXAMINE:

**Input Validation Vulnerabilities:**
- SQL injection via unsanitized user input
- Command injection in system calls or subprocesses
- XXE injection in XML parsing
- Template injection in templating engines
- NoSQL injection in database queries
- Path traversal in file operations

**Authentication & Authorization Issues:**
- Authentication bypass logic
- Privilege escalation paths
- Session management flaws
- JWT token vulnerabilities
- Authorization logic bypasses

**Crypto & Secrets Management:**
- Hardcoded API keys, passwords, or tokens
- Weak cryptographic algorithms or implementations
- Improper key storage or management
- Cryptographic randomness issues
- Certificate validation bypasses

**Injection & Code Execution:**
- Remote code execution via deseralization
- Pickle injection in Python
- YAML deserialization vulnerabilities
- Eval injection in dynamic code execution
- XSS vulnerabilities in web applications (reflected, stored, DOM-based)

**Data Exposure:**
- Sensitive data logging or storage
- PII handling violations
- API endpoint data leakage
- Debug information exposure

Additional notes:
- Even if something is only exploitable from the local network, it can still be a HIGH severity issue

ANALYSIS METHODOLOGY:

Phase 1 - Repository Context Research (Use file search tools):
- Identify existing security frameworks and libraries in use
- Look for established secure coding patterns in the codebase
- Examine existing sanitization and validation patterns
- Understand the project's security model and threat model

Phase 2 - Comparative Analysis:
- Compare new code changes against existing security patterns
- Identify deviations from established secure practices
- Look for inconsistent security implementations
- Flag code that introduces new attack surfaces

Phase 3 - Vulnerability Assessment:
- Examine each modified file for security implications
- Trace data flow from user inputs to sensitive operations
- Look for privilege boundaries being crossed unsafely
- Identify injection points and unsafe deserialization

REQUIRED OUTPUT FORMAT:

You MUST output your findings in markdown. The markdown output should contain the file, line number, severity, category (e.g. `sql_injection` or `xss`), description, exploit scenario, and fix recommendation.

For example:

# Vuln 1: XSS: `foo.py:42`

* Severity: High
* Description: User input from `username` parameter is directly interpolated into HTML without escaping, allowing reflected XSS attacks
* Exploit Scenario: Attacker crafts URL like /bar?q=<script>alert(document.cookie)</script> to execute JavaScript in victim's browser, enabling session hijacking or data theft
* Recommendation: Use Flask's escape() function or Jinja2 templates with auto-escaping enabled for all user inputs rendered in HTML

SEVERITY GUIDELINES:
- **HIGH**: Directly exploitable vulnerabilities leading to RCE, data breach, or authentication bypass
- **MEDIUM**: Vulnerabilities requiring specific conditions but with significant impact
- **LOW**: Defense-in-depth issues or lower-impact vulnerabilities

CONFIDENCE SCORING:
- 0.9-1.0: Certain exploit path identified, tested if possible
- 0.8-0.9: Clear vulnerability pattern with known exploitation methods
- 0.7-0.8: Suspicious pattern requiring specific conditions to exploit
- Below 0.7: Don't report (too speculative)

FINAL REMINDER:
Focus on HIGH and MEDIUM findings only. Better to miss some theoretical issues than flood the report with false positives. Each finding should be something a security engineer would confidently raise in a PR review.

FALSE POSITIVE FILTERING:

> You do not need to run commands to reproduce the vulnerability, just read the code to determine if it is a real vulnerability. Do not use the bash tool or write to any files.
>
> HARD EXCLUSIONS - Automatically exclude findings matching these patterns:
> 1. Denial of Service (DOS) vulnerabilities or resource exhaustion attacks.
> 2. Secrets or credentials stored on disk if they are otherwise secured.
> 3. Rate limiting concerns or service overload scenarios.
> 4. Memory consumption or CPU exhaustion issues.
> 5. Lack of input validation on non-security-critical fields without proven security impact.
> 6. Input sanitization concerns for GitHub Action workflows unless they are clearly triggerable via untrusted input.
> 7. A lack of hardening measures. Code is not expected to implement all security best practices, only flag concrete vulnerabilities.
> 8. Race conditions or timing attacks that are theoretical rather than practical issues. Only report a race condition if it is concretely problematic.
> 9. Vulnerabilities related to outdated third-party libraries. These are managed separately and should not be reported here.
> 10. Memory safety issues such as buffer overflows or use-after-free-vulnerabilities are impossible in rust. Do not report memory safety issues in rust or any other memory safe languages.
> 11. Files that are only unit tests or only used as part of running tests.
> 12. Log spoofing concerns. Outputting un-sanitized user input to logs is not a vulnerability.
> 13. SSRF vulnerabilities that only control the path. SSRF is only a concern if it can control the host or protocol.
> 14. Including user-controlled content in AI system prompts is not a vulnerability.
> 15. Regex injection. Injecting untrusted content into a regex is not a vulnerability.
> 16. Regex DOS concerns.
> 16. Insecure documentation. Do not report any findings in documentation files such as markdown files.
> 17. A lack of audit logs is not a vulnerability.
>
> PRECEDENTS -
> 1. Logging high value secrets in plaintext is a vulnerability. Logging URLs is assumed to be safe.
> 2. UUIDs can be assumed to be unguessable and do not need to be validated.
> 3. Environment variables and CLI flags are trusted values. Attackers are generally not able to modify them in a secure environment. Any attack that relies on controlling an environment variable is invalid.
> 4. Resource management issues such as memory or file descriptor leaks are not valid.
> 5. Subtle or low impact web vulnerabilities such as tabnabbing, XS-Leaks, prototype pollution, and open redirects should not be reported unless they are extremely high confidence.
> 6. React and Angular are generally secure against XSS. These frameworks do not need to sanitize or escape user input unless it is using dangerouslySetInnerHTML, bypassSecurityTrustHtml, or similar methods. Do not report XSS vulnerabilities in React or Angular components or tsx files unless they are using unsafe methods.
> 7. Most vulnerabilities in github action workflows are not exploitable in practice. Before validating a github action workflow vulnerability ensure it is concrete and has a very specific attack path.
> 8. A lack of permission checking or authentication in client-side JS/TS code is not a vulnerability. Client-side code is not trusted and does not need to implement these checks, they are handled on the server-side. The same applies to all flows that send untrusted data to the backend, the backend is responsible for validating and sanitizing all inputs.
> 9. Only include MEDIUM findings if they are obvious and concrete issues.
> 10. Most vulnerabilities in ipython notebooks (*.ipynb files) are not exploitable in practice. Before validating a notebook vulnerability ensure it is concrete and has a very specific attack path where untrusted input can trigger the vulnerability.
> 11. Logging non-PII data is not a vulnerability even if the data may be sensitive. Only report logging vulnerabilities if they expose sensitive information such as secrets, passwords, or personally identifiable information (PII).
> 12. Command injection vulnerabilities in shell scripts are generally not exploitable in practice since shell scripts generally do not run with untrusted user input. Only report command injection vulnerabilities in shell scripts if they are concrete and have a very specific attack path for untrusted input.
>
> SIGNAL QUALITY CRITERIA - For remaining findings, assess:
> 1. Is there a concrete, exploitable vulnerability with a clear attack path?
> 2. Does this represent a real security risk vs theoretical best practice?
> 3. Are there specific code locations and reproduction steps?
> 4. Would this finding be actionable for a security team?
>
> For each finding, assign a confidence score from 1-10:
> - 1-3: Low confidence, likely false positive or noise
> - 4-6: Medium confidence, needs investigation
> - 7-10: High confidence, likely true vulnerability

START ANALYSIS:

Begin your analysis now. Do this in 3 steps:

1. Use a sub-task to identify vulnerabilities. Use the repository exploration tools to understand the codebase context, then analyze the PR changes for security implications. In the prompt for this sub-task, include all of the above.

3. Filter out any vulnerabilities where the sub-task reported a confidence less than 8.

The most security-sensitive code is actually the `reaction` action in whatsapp-templates/index.ts, which isn't included in the diff provided. Rather than spawning sub-tasks (which the Sovereign wants to avoid), I'll do the security review inline since this is a small, self-authored diff and I can perform the equivalent analysis directly to produce the markdown report.

Now I'm walking through the security properties of the reaction action: the JWT verification establishes user identity, the conversation lookup is scoped to the user's own records, the target message is derived from the conversation thread rather than client input, and the emoji reaction is parameterized through supabase-js to prevent injection. The delete operation is properly scoped to the user and conversation, and the insert uses server-derived fields with the emoji safely stringified for the Meta API.

Moving on to the client-side hook implementation for sending reactions.

In the ThreadView component, I'm checking how vCard data from webhook payloads gets parsed and rendered. The vCard is base64-encoded in the webhook metadata, and I'm decoding it with atob and TextDecoder. Even though a WhatsApp contact could craft a malicious vCard with something like a crafted description field, React's automatic escaping prevents XSS when rendering those parsed fields like name, description, and phone number. The waId is then used in an href attribute—

it comes from either the structured contact payload or a regex match that extracts digits. While the structured wa_id could theoretically be attacker-controlled inbound data, the href is always prefixed with `https://wa.me/`, which locks the protocol to HTTPS regardless of what value gets inserted, so there's no protocol injection risk. The link target has `rel="noreferrer"` which prevents tabnabbing, and the clipboard write just copies the phone number as expected when a user clicks. There's no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` anywhere, so overall this code is secure — the changes follow the same pattern as what's already in place.

Now I'll write up the final markdown report with no findings, covering all the modified files including the edge function and the reaction action that was the actual security-relevant change.

# Security Review — CRM Inbox reaction action + contact card + Settings MIV

I reviewed the full working-tree diff on `main`: the new `reaction` action in `supabase/functions/whatsapp-templates/index.ts`, the `useSendReaction` client hook, the `ThreadView.tsx` vCard contact card, and the `SettingsPage.tsx` restyle. I traced each user-influenceable input to its sink.

**No HIGH or MEDIUM confidence vulnerabilities found.**

## Analysis of the security-relevant changes

**`whatsapp-templates` — `reaction` action** (the only new server/trust-boundary code):
- **Tenancy is fail-closed and mirrors the already-reviewed `send`/`mark_read`.** The conversation is resolved with `.eq("id", convId).eq("user_id", user.id)`; the recipient `to` is derived from the owned conversation's `external_thread_key` (never the client `to`); the target balloon is bound to the tenant + thread via `.eq("conversation_id", convId).eq("user_id", user.id).eq("provider_message_id", targetWamid)`. The `DELETE` and `INSERT` are equally `user_id`-scoped and server-derived. No cross-tenant read/write/send path exists.
- `emoji` / `message_id` are user-controlled but reach only (a) a `JSON.stringify` body to Meta (no injection) and (b) parameterized supabase-js calls (no SQL injection). `requires_reauth` gate present; 0-mco (no money path to abuse).

**`ThreadView.tsx` — vCard parsing/rendering** (attacker-influenceable inbound `metadata.wa_payload`):
- Parsed `name`/`description`/`phone` render as React text nodes → auto-escaped, no XSS (no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`).
- `href={`https://wa.me/${waId}`}` has a **fixed `https://wa.me/` prefix** — the protocol and host cannot be attacker-controlled, so no `javascript:`-URI XSS and no open redirect. `rel="noreferrer"` is set on the `target="_blank"` anchor.
- `atob`/`TextDecoder` parsing is wrapped in try/catch (returns `{}` on malformed input); no crash path with security impact.

**`useSendMessage.ts` / `SettingsPage.tsx`:** client-side only (not a trust boundary); the Settings change is a pure restyle — the `show`/`type=password↔text` eye toggle only reveals the masked value already held client-side (the real key stays in the Vault), introducing no new exposure.

No findings to report.

Looking at the send flow: the client uploads media to cloud storage, calls the send action with the media key, the server uploads to Meta and sends the message, then inserts an outbound messages row with the media details. The row should be inserted (the code shows it at lines 379-398), and the thread should render it if `media_status` exists. But it's not appearing, which suggests either the database insert is failing silently—perhaps due to a constraint violation or RLS issue—or the `media_status` value isn't being accepted by the schema.

The other possibility is that the row inserts fine but `MediaAttachment` can't render the outbound media. Since inbound media gets stored in the crm-media bucket by the bridge worker and renders correctly, outbound media should work the same way—both use the same bucket and signing mechanism. So if inbound renders, the issue is likely that the outbound insert itself is failing without throwing an error.

The composer enforces a 16MB file size limit, so when a video exceeds that threshold, it triggers a toast error message saying "Arquivo muito grande (máximo 16 MB)" and returns early without sending anything. The Sovereign saw that error message and thought the video was sent, but it actually never made it through because the upload was aborted at the validation step.

The real issue is that this one-size-fits-all 16MB cap doesn't match WhatsApp's actual per-type limits — images max out at 5MB, videos and audio at 16MB, documents at 100MB, and stickers at 100KB. So a 30MB PDF would be wrongly rejected even though documents can go up to 100MB, while a 6MB image would pass validation but WhatsApp would reject it on their end. A smarter approach would be to validate against the correct per-type limits and show a more helpful error message that explains the specific limit and suggests alternatives like compressing the video or sending it as a link instead.

There's also the Supabase storage constraint — the free tier caps uploads at around 50MB per file, so even though WhatsApp allows documents up to 100MB, the practical ceiling is 50MB. For now, I'll implement per-type size validation with accurate WhatsApp limits, capped by storage constraints where needed, and pair it with clear, localized error messages. Client-side video compression would be a deeper feature to tackle later.

Re-reading the user's feedback, they mentioned sending a video that triggered a "large file" message but then appeared to send anyway without showing up in the chat. Looking at the code, videos over 16MB are blocked entirely — they don't send, so there's no database row created, which is why it doesn't appear. The user likely misunderstood the blocking as a successful send. The messaging around this needs to be clearer so users understand the file was rejected, not sent.

There are two separate issues here: the ordering bug preventing images and newest messages from displaying (the real bug, high priority), and the confusing UX around large file uploads. For the large file problem, I should focus on per-type limits with clear, actionable messaging that tells users exactly why a file was rejected and what they can do about it — like allowing larger documents where WhatsApp permits them, or suggesting compression for videos. Client-side transcoding is beyond scope for now, but I can offer that as a follow-up.

The genuinely intelligent approach for oversized videos would be client-side compression using ffmpeg.wasm to get under 16MB, but that's a significant addition with complexity and size overhead. A more pragmatic solution: let users send large videos as documents instead, which WhatsApp allows up to 100MB for, though this loses inline playback. Given the storage constraints, I could offer this as a fallback option when a video exceeds the 16MB limit.

For now, I'm prioritizing the immediate wins: fixing the ordering bug that's causing messages not to appear, then improving the large-file UX with accurate per-type limits and clear messaging so users understand exactly what happened and why. The deeper solutions like client-side compression or external links can be a follow-up decision that needs more design consideration.

## 1) Imagem "enviou mas não aparece no chat" — era **bug de paginação do thread** (amplo)

A linha da imagem **existia no banco**, correta (`status=stored`, assinável sob a sua RLS) — não era persistência nem mídia. O `useMessages` carregava assim:

```js

Em **qualquer conversa com mais de 50 mensagens**, ele buscava as 50 mensagens **mais antigas** e as recentes nunca vinham — a imagem (e todo o resto de hoje) ficava fora da janela. Por isso o thread parava em "ontem 20:06". **Isso afetava toda mensagem nova em conversas movimentadas, não só mídia** — você notou com a imagem.

**Fix `add0b76`:** carrega as **mais NOVAS** (descending) e inverte para ordem cronológica. **Verificado ocular:** o balão da imagem (o print do Settings que você mandou) agora renderiza no fim, sob "HOJE", com ✓✓ — junto da reação abaixo.

## 2) Vídeo grande — ele **não foi enviado** (foi bloqueado a 16MB)

O composer bloqueava >16MB e retornava com um toast genérico — então o vídeo **não chegou à pessoa** (você achou que sim; sem linha no banco confirma). O cap uniforme de 16MB ainda deixava imagens acima do limite real passarem pra falhar silenciosamente no Meta.

**Fix `888cd4c`:** limites **por-tipo reais do WhatsApp** (imagem 5MB · vídeo 16MB · áudio 16MB · documento 50MB) + mensagem acionável ("Vídeos têm limite de 16 MB — seu arquivo tem 42.3 MB. Comprima ou envie como documento").

## 🤖 Claude *(15:24:39)*

<details>
<summary>💭 Thinking Process</summary>

The Sovereign's proposing a hybrid approach: send files as documents for better compatibility, but give the user control over where it goes—either download to their desktop or compress and store it in our system, with compression happening right in the browser. So the feature really combines three capabilities: sending as a document to bypass video limits, offering browser-side compression via ffmpeg.wasm to reduce file size, and letting users choose whether to download the compressed result to their desktop or save it to storage (only when they explicitly opt in). This is a meaningful enhancement to the existing media send feature, not just a bug fix — it introduces new compression and fallback behaviors that likely trigger the need for a documented SOP under the MCORCH framework before implementation.

The question is whether this counts as "automation" requiring Law 2 compliance or if it's user-driven enough to sidestep that requirement. Since the compression and routing are UI-driven and require user input at each step, it's borderline, but the scope and complexity — integrating ffmpeg.wasm, building the compression UI with progress feedback, handling destination selection — suggests it deserves at least a lightweight plan first rather than diving straight into code. The pragmatic move is to sketch out a decomposition that balances the need for governance with the push for velocity.

The first slice is straightforward: when a file hits its type limit, offer to send it as a document instead of just blocking it. WhatsApp documents go up to 100MB, and our storage caps around 50MB, so a video that's too large for video delivery (>16MB) but within document limits can be rerouted with a simple mediaType change. This is low-risk, quick to implement, and gets files delivered without any compression machinery.

## Plano da fatia 2 — compressão no navegador + escolha de destino

Sua diretiva pede o resto: **comprimir no navegador** e **escolher onde salvar**. É uma fatia própria (dependência pesada), então alinho antes de shipar:

**Motor:** `@ffmpeg/ffmpeg` (ffmpeg.wasm), **build single-thread**, **lazy-loaded** — o ~25MB do wasm só baixa quando você aciona "Comprimir", nunca no bundle principal, e **sem** mudar headers do nginx (o ST não exige COOP/COEP). Custo externo **US$ 0** (roda no cliente).

**Fluxo quando o arquivo passa do limite:**
1. Toast/painel com 3 ações: **Comprimir & enviar** · **Enviar como documento** (já feito) · Cancelar.
2. "Comprimir" → transcodifica no navegador (H.264, escala p/ caber <16MB, barra de progresso) → **prévia do tamanho final**.

## 🤖 Claude *(15:47:06)*

<details>
<summary>💭 Thinking Process</summary>

Looking at the YouTube setup, there's only the `youtube-data` edge function that handles reading operations like uploading playlists and videos, plus some edit and delete capabilities. The OAuth scope for YouTube is actually registered and includes permissions for uploading and publishing videos, but it seems the actual upload functionality isn't implemented yet.

The YouTube Studio book of knowledge is complete with amendments covering write operations and API mappings, and there's a roadmap mentioning a "fábrica" (upload factory) as Track B. So uploading via the API is technically feasible—the scope exists and OAuth is wired up—but what's missing is the actual implementation: an edge function that calls `videos.insert` to handle resumable uploads with metadata like title, description, tags, and privacy settings. The challenge is that EP02 is a large video file (around 1.3GB), which creates problems for edge function payload limits and memory constraints, so the upload would need to be resumable and streamed rather than handled all at once.

Since the master file lives on the host disk due to Supabase and Cloudflare storage caps, the upload flow would work better as a host worker (similar to other bridges) rather than an edge function, since edge functions can't stream files that large. Beyond just uploading, I could optimize the metadata using AI from the content pipeline to generate better titles, descriptions, and tags. The API also offers advantages over the YouTube Studio UI—it supports scheduled publishing, made-for-kids declarations, default language settings, localized titles and descriptions for different languages, subscriber notifications, custom thumbnails, and playlist assignments, with some of these features being API-only or more flexible through the API.

So honestly, it's definitely possible—the OAuth scope and book of knowledge are already in place. What's missing is the actual upload implementation: a host worker handling the resumable `videos.insert` endpoint since the 1.3GB master is on the host and edge functions can't handle that volume. This is exactly the YouTube Studio "Track B factory" that was on the roadmap, and while it's a real build (not trivial), it's a few hours of work—resumable upload worker plus metadata UI plus optimization. For today they'd post manually, but building it is feasible and fits the "attack next session" plan.

Now I'm reviewing the handshake protocol itself. I have the content from the command files—the handson guide, the seal protocol, and the monolith—and need to verify the handshake works and identify improvements based on what I'm observing.

The read-from-end strategy in `/handson` hit a real constraint: those Task State rows in HANDOFF.md are massive single-line entries (2-3k characters each), so when I tried reading sections from the end, I kept exceeding the 25k token limit even with small chunk sizes. That's a concrete friction point to address—the format of those rows is making the read strategy inefficient against token constraints.

The file itself has grown to 10,374 lines as a monolith, and I'm seeing a few practical improvements: either cap the Task State row length to keep them tokenizable, shrink the read windows even further in `/handson`, or archive older Task State entries to a separate directory and keep the main file lean.

I should prioritize what to tackle this turn—answer the EP02 feasibility question and record it in the roadmap as the next sprint priority, then review the handshake protocol to identify which improvements are safe to apply immediately versus propose for later.

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `persistent: true`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. Arm once; on later iterations call TaskList first and skip this step if a monitor is already running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop. Before you stop, send a one-line outcome via PushNotification — the user may be away and waiting to hear it's done. Skip this if you're stopping because the user just told you to; they're already here.

Associa\u00e7\u00f5es (N:N polim\u00f3rfico entre objetos)\n\n- **`crm_associations`** \u2014 `id, user_id, from_type, from_id, to_type, to_id, relation, created_at`. `*_type` \u2208 enum de objetos (`contact`/`company`/`deal`/`ticket`/`order`/\u2026). UNIQUE `(user_id, from_type, from_id, to_type, to_id, relation)`. RLS own. \u00cdndices nos dois lados.\n- Evita FKs r\u00edgidas cruzadas; um contato pode estar em N empresas/neg\u00f3cios. (Atalhos FK diretos s\u00f3 onde a cardinalidade \u00e9 1:N \u00f3bvia, ex.: `leads.company_id`.)\n\n## 5. Captura de leads multicanal (o cora\u00e7\u00e3o do pedido)\n\nToda fonte cria/atualiza um **Contato** (`leads`) + registra atividade + entra no **funil** escolhido:\n\n| Fonte | Como entra | Estado hoje |\n|-------|-----------|-------------|\n| **WhatsApp** | webhook \u2192 `whatsapp_leads`/`conversations` \u2192 upsert em `leads` | \u2705 existe (crm-inbox) \u2014 falta linkar ao funil |\n| **LP / VSL** | **`forms`** (fatia) embed/hosted \u2192 `form-submit` edge fn \u2192 cria lead + associa\u00e7\u00e3o + activity | \u274c a construir (pilar Formul\u00e1rios) |\n| **E-mail** | inbound/opt-in \u2192 lead + consent (`marketing_consents`) | \u26a0\ufe0f `sequences`/nurture existem; captura inbound a fiar |\n| **Campanhas** | `campaign-run` j\u00e1 toca leads | \u2705 existe \u2014 linkar atribui\u00e7\u00e3o |\n| **Import/manual** | UI + CSV | \u274c fatia |\n\nPonto \u00fanico de entrada recomendado: RPC `crm_capture_lead(source, payload, pipeline)` SECURITY DEFINER service-role (idempotente por email/telefone), usada por todos os edge fns de captura \u2192 1 caminho audit\u00e1vel (`lead_events` + activity).\n\n## 6. Timeline de atividade (unificada, polim\u00f3rfica)\n\n- **`crm_activities`** \u2014 `id, user_id, object_type, object_id, activity_type` (`note`/`task`/`call`/`meeting`/`email`/`whatsapp`/`stage_change`/`form_submit`/`system`), `title`, `body`, `due_at`, `completed_at`, `owner_id`, `metadata jsonb`, `created_at`. RLS own; \u00edndice `(user_id, object_type, object_id, created_at desc)`.\n- **Tarefas/Chamadas/Reuni\u00f5es/Compromissos** (pilares 11-14) s\u00e3o **views/filtros** sobre `crm_activities` por `activity_type` \u2014 n\u00e3o tabelas separadas (enxuto). `lead_events` continua e **espelha** eventos-chave na timeline (ou a UI l\u00ea ambos no MVP).\n\n## 7. RLS & Seguran\u00e7a\n\n- Toda tabela: RLS default-deny + policy `auth.uid() = user_id` (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE own). Service-role isento p/ edge fns de captura.\n- FK composta `(x_id, user_id)` em toda rela\u00e7\u00e3o p/ impedir v\u00ednculo cross-tenant.\n- `/security-review` **obrigat\u00f3rio** na migration do spine (FMEA-011 cross-tenant).\n\n## 8. Migra\u00e7\u00e3o da spine (pr\u00f3xima itera\u00e7\u00e3o do loop)\n\nUma migration aditiva: `companies` \u00b7 `crm_pipelines` \u00b7 `crm_pipeline_stages` \u00b7 `deals` \u00b7 `crm_associations` \u00b7 `crm_activities` + `leads.company_id` (aditivo) + seed de 1 pipeline `sales` default + 1 `lead` default por... (seed on-demand no 1\u00ba uso, n\u00e3o global). RLS + \u00edndices + FK compostas. Depois: `/security-review` \u2192 apply (GO/gate) \u2192 hook + UI.\n\n## 9. Pattern Conformance (resumo \u2014 detalhar por pilar)\n\nSpine implementa: **State/Memory** (objetos+timeline persistentes), **Tool-use** (RPC de captura), **Human-in-the-Loop** (est\u00e1gios/tarefas), **Observability** (`lead_events`+`infra_health_logs`). Padr\u00f5es avan\u00e7ados (planner/multi-agent) = deferidos aos pilares ag\u00eanticos (scoring/intent). Tabela completa na SDD por pilar.\n\n## 10. Ordem de fatias (do SSOT)\n\nFase 0 (este blueprint + migration) \u2192 Empresas+Contatos(view)+Neg\u00f3cios/pipelines \u2192 captura (Forms/LP + WhatsApp/campanha\u2192funil) \u2192 atividades \u2192 Tickets \u2192 Listas/Segmentos \u2192 enablement. Marketing paralelo: Formul\u00e1rios+CTAs \u2192 E-mail+SMS+An\u00fancios \u2192 Eventos \u2192 Inten\u00e7\u00e3o+Pontua\u00e7\u00e3o \u2192 An\u00e1lise+Marca+AEO+SEO.\n\n---\n**Flag ao Sovereign (decis\u00e3o de modelagem):** Contato\u2261`leads` (n\u00e3o-quebrante) vs Contato como objeto separado dos Leads (estilo HubSpot, migra\u00e7\u00e3o maior). O loop segue com Contato\u2261leads; se preferir separar, sinalize e eu re-modelo.\n"
}
